title: Gathered remembrance
hookLine: circles of dhikr, sung or silent

lines: A ROOM THAT RISES LIKE SURF.
cards: The same Thursday night, two rooms. In the first, in a city in Morocco or Egypt, people sit shoulder to shoulder in a circle.
Someone begins a phrase and the whole room takes it up, rocking gently, the sound rising and falling like surf, for an hour.
In the second, somewhere in Central Asia or Turkey, people sit in a circle too, heads bowed, eyes closed. Nobody makes a sound. The only sound is breathing.
Ask either room what it's doing, and you'd get the same answer.

teach.b: The thing is dhikr: remembrance of God, usually by repeating short phrases. La ilaha illa Allah, there is no god but God. Subhan Allah, glory be to God.
Or simply Allah. You've met dhikr before on this path: a Muslim who says these after prayer is already doing it. What the orders added was the circle, the halqah, remembrance done together.
Some circles say it aloud, sometimes with singing and a drum. That's jahri, out loud. Others, like the Naqshbandis, keep it silent, in the heart.
Both point to the same verse, in Pickthall's words: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
And to a hadith in Sahih Muslim: whenever people sit together remembering God, the angels surround them, mercy covers them, calm descends on them, and God mentions them to those who are with Him.

In another, in al-Bukhari, God says, in a hadith qudsi: if my servant remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than that.
Muslims do differ here. Some scholars object to group dhikr in unison or with music, seeing it as later than the Prophet's practice; others defend it. More on that in two days.
But the silent circle points at the heart of it all: the tongue can say the words, but the goal is that the heart says them. The heart says it.

how: Muslims remember God with short phrases after prayer and throughout the day, often counting on the fingers or prayer beads; in Sufi orders, members also gather in circles of dhikr, aloud or silent, while some scholars object to group dhikr in unison.

o: a reunion where families recall loved ones who died
a yearly feast honoring a Sufi order's founder
remembering God together, aloud or in silence

s: anyone who says these phrases after prayer is doing it. the orders added the circle.
some sing and drum; others, like the Naqshbandis, keep it silent.
a hadith says angels surround people who gather to remember God
and mercy covers them, and calm descends on them.

games.q: you walk into a Naqshbandi circle. nobody makes a sound. what are they doing?
o: waiting for the shaykh to arrive.
silent dhikr: remembering God in the heart.
games.why: khafi dhikr, hidden remembrance: the tongue still, the heart saying it.

practice: Sit, eyes closed if you like, and let your breath settle into its own pace.
If you pray, say a phrase silently with each breath, inside, not with your lips: Allah on the breath in, Allah on the breath out, or la ilaha illa Allah across one breath.
If you don't pray, rest on the breath alone, counting it or simply following it, and let the heart do the saying.

wordCard.voice: Gathered remembrance. Circles of dhikr, sung aloud or held in silence, remembering God together. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: remembrance, mention; the repetition of short phrases remembering God.

carryVoice: Your line: the heart says it. Even when the tongue is still. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!
